title: Diagnostic Performance of Urinary CD163 as a Non-invasive Biomarker for Egyptian Lupus Nephritis Patients Versus Conventional Biomarkers
off: Diagnostic Performance of Urinary CD163 as a Non-invasive Biomarker for Egyptian Lupus Nephritis Patients Versus Conventional Biomarkers

This prospective observational study aims to evaluate the potential of urinary soluble CD163 (uCD163) as a non-invasive biomarker for predicting renal remission in patients with lupus nephritis. desc:
Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and an important cause of progressive kidney damage and kidney failure. Assessment of renal disease activity and prediction of treatment response remain challenging because conventional clinical and laboratory markers, including proteinuria, serum creatinine, complement levels, and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, may not accurately reflect ongoing inflammation within the kidney.

CD163 is a receptor expressed mainly on macrophages involved in inflammatory processes. Its soluble form can be released into the circulation and urine. Urinary soluble CD163 (uCD163) is a potential non-invasive biomarker of renal inflammation and may provide additional information about disease activity, histopathological findings, and response to immunosuppressive treatment.

This study is designed as a prospective longitudinal observational cohort study conducted at Assiut University Hospitals, involving the Nephrology and Rheumatology Units of the Internal Medicine Department. Adult patients with biopsy-proven active lupus nephritis requiring immunosuppressive treatment will be enrolled and followed for six months.

At baseline, demographic and clinical information will be collected, including age, sex, duration of SLE, relevant medical history, clinical manifestations, current medications, and previous immunosuppressive treatment. Renal biopsy findings will be reviewed to determine the histopathological class according to the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classification, together with the histological activity and chronicity indices.

Urinary soluble CD163 will be measured at baseline and at weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, and 24. Urinary CD163 levels will be assessed in relation to urinary creatinine to account for variations in urine concentration. The laboratory assessment will also include serial measurements of proteinuria, serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), complement components C3 and C4, and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies. Additional investigations will include complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, as clinically indicated.

Patients will receive standard-of-care immunosuppressive treatment according to their treating physicians' decisions and established clinical practice guidelines. Treatment will not be assigned or modified by the study protocol. The therapeutic approach will include induction therapy aimed at controlling active renal inflammation and achieving remission, followed by maintenance immunosuppression to preserve renal response and reduce the risk of relapse. Treatment details will be documented, including the immunosuppressive agents used, doses, administration schedules, treatment duration, glucocorticoid exposure, dose adjustments, and any changes due to inadequate response, adverse effects, or clinical deterioration. Relevant medications may include glucocorticoids, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors, and other guideline-based therapies when clinically indicated.

Clinical and laboratory parameters, together with serial urinary CD163 measurements, will be assessed throughout the follow-up period to evaluate changes in renal disease activity and treatment response. The relationship between baseline urinary CD163 levels, early changes during treatment, histopathological findings, and subsequent clinical response will be investigated.

The study will evaluate whether urinary soluble CD163 can serve as a useful non-invasive biomarker for predicting renal remission and monitoring treatment response in patients with lupus nephritis. It will also explore the relationship between urinary CD163 and traditional clinical, laboratory, and histopathological indicators of renal disease activity, with the aim of improving disease monitoring and supporting more accurate assessment of treatment response.
elig:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Adults aged 18 years or older.
* Diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) according to the 2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria.
* Diagnosis of lupus nephritis according to the ACR criteria.
* Biopsy-proven lupus nephritis.
* Adequate renal biopsy tissue available for histopathological classification and assessment of activity and chronicity indices.
* Active lupus nephritis requiring induction or escalation of immunosuppressive treatment.
* Availability of baseline laboratory investigations.
* Ability to provide a urine sample for urinary soluble CD163 measurement.

Exclusion Criteria:

* Chronic kidney disease unrelated to systemic lupus erythematosus.
* Recent infection or acute inflammatory condition.
* Previous kidney transplantation.
* Active urinary tract infection at the time of urine sampling.
* Severe infection requiring hospitalization or intravenous antimicrobial treatment at baseline.
* Malignancy or another major inflammatory disease that could significantly affect urinary CD163 levels.
* Inadequate renal biopsy specimen for histopathological assessment.

arms.d: Group (I): 30 participants with histologically proven class III, IV, V or any combination of these classes of active LN.
Group (II): 10 patients with active SLE (SLEDAI \> 6) without nephritis confirmed by the absence of albuminuria or microscopic haematuria
Group (III): 10 participants with non-active SLE (SLEDAI score \<2).

primary.m: Primary (main): Earliest the earliest biochemical level change as a marker of remission/relapse/response to treatment
